opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think activism plays a really important role, and I'd put it this way: activists have been very good at identifying problems and raising alarms. A lot of the attention that algorithmic fairness, privacy, and accountability get today exists because journalists, advocates, and affected communities pointed out real harms, like biased risk assessment tools in criminal justice, discriminatory ad delivery, and facial recognition systems that perform worse on certain groups. That pressure gets companies and regulators to take these issues seriously, and I don't want to minimize it at all.

Where I think there's sometimes a gap is between identifying a problem and fixing it. Once you sit down to actually build a fairer or more private algorithm, you have to be extremely precise about what you mean. What does "fair" mean? Fair to which groups? Measured by false positive rates, false negative rates, overall accuracy? We know from the theoretical literature that some of these definitions are mutually incompatible. You can't satisfy all of them at once. And almost any fairness constraint costs you something, usually some predictive accuracy. So there are real tradeoffs, and somebody has to decide where on that tradeoff curve society wants to sit.

That's where I think the two communities can complement each other. The scientists and developers can make the tradeoffs explicit and quantitative. We can show you that here's the Pareto frontier between error and unfairness, and here are the options. But choosing among those options is not purely a technical question. It's a question of values and policy, and that's exactly where activists, stakeholders, and the people affected by these systems should have a strong voice.

So I'd say activism is most productive when it engages with that level of specificity, not just "this algorithm is biased, stop using it," but "here's the harm we care about most, here's the group we're worried about, and here's the cost we're willing to accept to reduce it." And developers, for their part, should welcome that input rather than treating it as an adversarial thing. The worst outcome is when each side talks past the other, with activists frustrated that engineers don't care and engineers frustrated that the critiques aren't actionable. The best outcome is a real dialogue where the moral concerns get translated into precise objectives that we can actually build into the algorithms.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think there's an important distinction to draw here, and it's one that Aaron Roth and I tried to make in the book. Activism, in the sense of people raising alarms about the ways that algorithms are being deployed in lending or criminal sentencing or hiring, has been enormously valuable. A lot of the problems that researchers now work on, including in fairness and privacy, were really surfaced first by journalists and advocates and affected communities, not by computer scientists. So I don't want to minimize that at all. It's a necessary part of the ecosystem.

But I'd say activism, on its own, is not a design methodology. If you're a developer sitting down to build a model that's going to make consequential decisions about people, it's not enough to have good intentions or to have read the critiques. You need precise definitions of what you mean by fairness, or privacy, or whatever the value is, and you need algorithms that are actually constrained to respect those definitions. And one of the uncomfortable things you learn when you do that is that these values are often in tension with each other, and with accuracy. Choosing how to trade them off is not a technical question. That's a societal question, and that's exactly where activism and public debate should be feeding in.

So the way I'd put it is this. The role of activists and regulators and the broader public is to help decide what we want, what constraints matter, who we're worried about harming. The role of the developer is to make sure that once those decisions are made, they're actually embedded in the code rather than in a mission statement. Where it goes wrong is when either side tries to do the other's job. Developers shouldn't be unilaterally deciding what fairness means for society, and advocates shouldn't assume that saying "be fair" is sufficient to make an algorithm fair. The science of putting these principles into algorithms is still young, but I think it's the bridge between the two.

astra-6.text:
I think activism has an important role to play, especially when it comes from the people actually building these systems. Developers are often in a position to see risks that aren’t visible to the public, and they should be able to raise concerns and push back on uses they find objectionable.

But I wouldn’t want responsible AI to depend entirely on individual developers taking a stand. If an organization says it values privacy or fairness, those commitments need to show up in the development process: What are we measuring? What constraints are we imposing? Who has the authority to stop a deployment when those constraints aren’t met?

Activism can help create the pressure to put those mechanisms in place. Technical work can make some of the commitments precise and testable. Neither replaces the other, and neither eliminates the need for accountability at the organizational level.

sol-6.1.text:
I think activism has an important role to play, especially when there’s a gap between the principles an organization announces and the decisions it actually makes. Developers are often in a position to see that gap before anybody outside the organization can. They understand what the technology can do, where it fails, and what pressures are shaping its deployment.

But we shouldn’t put the entire burden on individual developers to take a principled stand at considerable personal risk. Responsible AI needs institutional support: ways to raise concerns, meaningful review processes, and people with the authority to change or stop a project. Otherwise, a statement of principles doesn’t give you much protection when it conflicts with a business objective.

So I see activism as complementary to the technical work. You can develop methods for making systems more fair or more private, but those methods don’t decide whether the organization will use them. Activism can help create the pressure and accountability that make those commitments meaningful.
